domain.name: Software Architecture
domain.description: Decoupled event streaming, microservice resilience, CQRS, and domain-driven design.

domainCoverage.synopsis: System architecture comprises the decisions that are expensive to reverse. This volume explores decoupled message streaming, bounded contexts, and circuit breakers.

chapters.title: Modular Monolith Design
chapters.summary: Structure a single deployable binary into strictly isolated domain modules with enforced public APIs and private schemas—gaining clean boundaries without network tax.

chapters.title: Microservices Decomposition
chapters.summary: Split a system along business capability and transactional consistency boundaries, not technical layers or entity nouns.

chapters.title: DDD Strategic Context Mapping
chapters.summary: Explicitly defining bounded contexts, their ubiquitous language boundaries, and the upstream/downstream integration relationships between teams and services in a complex domain.

chapters.title: DDD Tactical Patterns
chapters.summary: Building-block patterns—Entities, Value Objects, Aggregates, Domain Events, and Repositories—that encapsulate business invariants inside clear transactional consistency boundaries.

chapters.title: Hexagonal Architecture
chapters.summary: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where all external I/O—HTTP, SQL, queues, third-party APIs—plugs in through interfaces owned by the domain.

chapters.title: Onion Architecture
chapters.summary: An architectural style that places domain entities and business rules at the center, forcing all dependencies—frameworks, databases, and UI—to point strictly inward through interfaces.

chapters.title: CQRS & Event Sourcing
chapters.summary: CQRS separates write-side command validation from read-side query projections, while Event Sourcing persists every state transition as an immutable append-only log of domain events rather than overwriting current rows.

chapters.title: Consumer-Driven Contract Testing & Chaos Engineering
chapters.summary: Combining Consumer-Driven Contract Testing (schema and state compatibility) with Chaos Engineering (fault injection, latency, and packet loss) to prove distributed services neither miscommunicate nor cascade-fail under stress.

chapters.title: GraphQL Federation
chapters.summary: GraphQL Federation composes multiple independent domain subgraphs into a single unified schema at a stateless router, letting teams deploy services separately while clients query one endpoint.

chapters.title: Serverless & FaaS Design
chapters.summary: Serverless Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) executes stateless, event-driven handlers in ephemeral sandboxes—such as Firecracker microVMs (AWS Lambda) or V8 isolates (Cloudflare Workers)—scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent instances per second with per-millisecond billing. Designing for FaaS requires bounding cold starts, decoupling slow downstream dependencies via queues, and preventing connection-pool exhaustion.

chapters.title: Database Sharding & Range Partitioning
chapters.summary: Horizontally partitioning a dataset across independent database nodes by a shard key—using either contiguous key ranges or consistent hashing—to scale write throughput and storage beyond a single primary's CPU, IOPS, and memory ceiling.

chapters.title: Poison Message Handling
chapters.summary: Poison message handling isolates unprocessable queue or stream messages—caused by malformed payloads, schema drift, or deterministic business-rule bugs—so they do not loop infinitely and starve healthy traffic.

chapters.title: Chaos Engineering
chapters.summary: Chaos engineering is the disciplined practice of injecting controlled, hypothesis-driven faults—like AZ blackholes, 200 ms packet delay, or Redis evictions—into production-like systems to uncover hidden fragility before real outages do.

domainDeepDive.whatIsThisDomain: Software architecture comprises the high-level structural decisions, boundary definitions, and communication contracts that govern how systems are built, decomposed, and evolved. It establishes how business capabilities map to software components, how state and transactional ownership are partitioned across domain boundaries, and how non-functional requirements (scalability, security, maintainability, and fault isolation) are satisfied throughout the software lifecycle.
domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Software architecture encompasses the decisions that are perilous and expensive to change once systems reach production. An architecture misaligned with organizational domain boundaries creates distributed monoliths—architectures that suffer the extreme operational complexity of distributed networks while retaining the catastrophic coupling of monolithic systems. Correct architecture provides clear boundaries of change, enabling dozens of autonomous teams to ship features continuously without coordination bottlenecks.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: Optimize architecture for loose coupling, clear data ownership, and reversibility. The best architecture is not the one that predicts the future, but the one that makes changing your mind inexpensive.
coreArchitectureRules: Conway's Law Invariant: Software system architectures inevitably mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them. Align system boundaries with autonomous team boundaries.

Single Source of Truth & Data Sovereignty: Each microservice or bounded context must exclusively own its underlying database schema. Direct database sharing across service boundaries is strictly prohibited.

The End-to-End Argument: Lower-level system components cannot anticipate all higher-level semantic requirements. Crucial application guarantees (such as transactional deduplication and data integrity) must be validated end-to-end at the application layer.

Postel's Robustness Principle: Be conservative in what you send, and liberal in what you accept. Services must tolerate additive schema changes (backward and forward compatibility) without deployment locks.

Fault Domain Isolation: Every architectural boundary must establish an explicit fault barrier. Failure in an analytics or recommendation subsystem must never degrade core checkout or authentication paths.

failureModes.name: The Distributed Monolith Trap
failureModes.description: Decomposing an application into 40 microservices that share a single relational database and require synchronous lockstep deployments, multiplying network latency without delivering team autonomy.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict domain boundaries using Domain-Driven Design (DDD). Decouple schemas into private datastores and communicate exclusively through versioned APIs or event streams.

failureModes.name: Chatty Distributed Query Cascades (N+1 Across Microservices)
failureModes.description: A frontend endpoint calls an aggregator service, which in turn performs sequential loops of RPC calls to multiple downstream microservices to assemble a single response, multiplying latency by N.
failureModes.mitigation: Employ CQRS read-model projections, GraphQL Federation with batching (DataLoader), or asynchronous materialized views populated via event streams.

failureModes.name: Schema Drift & Breaking Contract Deployments
failureModes.description: A producer service modifies an API response field or deletes an enum value, instantly breaking hundreds of downstream consumer services that lacked contract tests.
failureModes.mitigation: Implement consumer-driven contract testing (Pact) in CI pipelines and enforce schema evolution registries (Protobuf/Avro) that prohibit breaking field deletions.

failureModes.name: Shared Database Anti-Pattern
failureModes.description: Multiple services run direct SQL queries against tables owned by another team. Schema migrations by one team silently crash background workers in other domains.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce API encapsulation. Convert shared tables into private domain models accessible only via gRPC/REST APIs or published domain events.

whenToUse: Large engineering organizations with multiple autonomous product teams needing independent deployment cadences.
Complex business domains with distinct sub-domains (e.g. payment processing, order fulfillment, catalog search) that scale and evolve at different speeds.
Systems requiring disparate non-functional characteristics (e.g. streaming telemetry requiring high write throughput vs checkout requiring strict ACID linearizability).
Applications transitioning from a monolithic legacy core to modular services using Strangler Fig migrations.
whenNotToUse: Early-stage MVPs where business requirements and domain boundaries are rapidly shifting weekly; a well-factored Modular Monolith is 10x faster to iterate on.
Small development teams (fewer than 10-15 engineers) where the operational tax of microservices (Kubernetes, service meshes, distributed tracing) drains development velocity.
Workloads with deeply intertwined relational queries requiring low-latency transactions across hundreds of foreign keys.
CRUD applications with minimal business logic that simply proxy requests to a relational database.

tradeOffs.pro: Modular monoliths provide zero network latency, single-repository refactoring, and simple atomic database transactions.
tradeOffs.con: All modules share a single deployment runtime, scaling envelope, and technology stack, limiting deployment independence for large teams.

tradeOffs.pro: Centralized orchestrators (Temporal / Step Functions) provide explicit, easily audited state machines and end-to-end visibility.
tradeOffs.con: Orchestrators create a centralized coupling point and can become an architectural bottleneck if overused.

tradeOffs.pro: gRPC delivers high-efficiency binary serialization (Protobuf) and typed contracts ideal for internal East-West microservice traffic.
tradeOffs.con: gRPC requires specialized tooling, lacks native browser support without grpc-web proxies, and is harder to inspect than JSON/REST.

productionScenarios.title: Strangler Fig Migration of Legacy Core Banking
productionScenarios.scenario: A 15-year-old monolithic core banking application blocked cloud migration and took 6 hours to build and deploy. Downtime risk was unacceptable.
productionScenarios.outcome: Implemented an API Gateway routing layer that intercepted incoming customer traffic, redirecting new loan origination flows to modern microservices while strangling legacy modules incrementally, achieving zero downtime across a 14-month phased rollout.

productionScenarios.title: CQRS Read-Optimized View for E-Commerce Catalog
productionScenarios.scenario: High-traffic Black Friday sales caused massive database lock contention on inventory tables because write transactions blocked millions of read queries.
productionScenarios.outcome: Split write commands from read queries using CQRS. Write commands update the relational inventory source of truth, while an event bus projects changes into read-optimized Elasticsearch indices, cutting catalog latency from 450ms to 9ms.

coreChallenges.title: Conway's Law & Team Boundaries
coreChallenges.explanation: System designs inevitably mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them. Misaligned organizational boundaries produce mismatched system interfaces and cross-team deployment bottlenecks.

coreChallenges.title: Microservices Decomposition & Data Coupling
coreChallenges.explanation: Decomposing a system along entity boundaries rather than transaction and domain boundaries creates chatty distributed joins, distributed transactions, and cascading latency traps.

coreChallenges.title: Bounded Contexts & Ubiquitous Language
coreChallenges.explanation: A customer in billing is fundamentally different from a customer in shipping. Without explicit Domain-Driven Design (DDD) context mappings, shared models bleed across domains, creating unmaintainable dependencies.

coreChallenges.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Coupling
coreChallenges.explanation: Synchronous RPC cascades availability failures across downstream services. Asynchronous event-driven choreography isolates failures and decouples services in time, space, and deployment cadence.

domainDeepDive.architecturalMindset: Senior software architects optimize for reversibility and loose coupling over speculative scalability. They draw strict data boundaries, treat network calls as failure points, and ensure each bounded context can evolve and deploy independently.

domainContent.title: Software Architecture

spark.summary: Software architecture is the set of high-level decisions that shape how a system is divided, how its parts communicate, and how it changes over time.
spark.keyTakeaway: Good architecture makes changing your mind less expensive. Start with clear boundaries, explicit ownership, and controlled communication.

domain.purpose: Learn to design software systems that remain understandable, changeable, scalable, and resilient as teams, traffic, and business requirements grow.
audience: Software engineers preparing for system design interviews.
Engineers decomposing monoliths or designing service boundaries.
Technical leads making long-term architecture decisions.
learningOutcomes: Choose distribution only when it provides a concrete benefit.
Reason about data ownership, consistency, and communication.
Design failure behavior before an incident.
Keep business rules independent of infrastructure.
Use operational evidence to evolve a system.

learningJourney.title: Understand architectural boundaries
learningJourney.purpose: Learn what architecture is and why boundaries matter.
learningJourney.explanation: Architecture shapes where responsibilities live, how components interact, and which decisions are expensive to reverse. Its quality is not the number of services; it is how well the structure supports the system's requirements.

ideas.title: Cohesion
ideas.description: Keep behavior and data that enforce the same business rules close together. Changes to one business capability should not require touching unrelated parts of the application.

ideas.title: Coupling
ideas.description: A dependency becomes costly when its consumer must understand internal details or coordinate every change. Prefer explicit, narrow contracts over shared implementation knowledge.

example.title: Ordering is not payment processing
example.scenario: Ordering owns order status and line items. Payments owns charges, refunds, and provider interactions.
example.reasoning: They may start as modules in one application, but each should have a clear responsibility and interface.
example.lesson: A boundary separates ownership and change, not merely database tables.

reflectionQuestions: Which responsibilities change together?
Who owns the data needed to enforce each rule?
Which operations need a single transaction?
Which failures should remain independent?

learningJourney.title: Design for change
learningJourney.purpose: Learn how to preserve flexibility as a system and organization evolve.
learningJourney.explanation: A modular monolith can provide strong boundaries, one deployment, and straightforward transactions. Extract a service when independent ownership, scaling, release cadence, or fault isolation creates a concrete benefit.

ideas.title: Make decisions visible
ideas.description: An architecture decision record captures context, alternatives, the chosen approach, its consequences, and evidence that might cause the decision to be revisited.

ideas.title: Keep options open
ideas.description: Use migration seams, compatible contracts, and staged rollouts when uncertainty is meaningful. Reversibility has value, but abstractions also have a cost.

example.title: Reporting outgrows the main application
example.scenario: Heavy reports compete with checkout for resources.
example.reasoning: First isolate reporting behind an interface and measure the bottleneck. Then build a separate read model, compare outputs, gradually route requests, and retain a rollback path.
example.lesson: Extract to solve a measured problem, not to satisfy a service-count target.

reflectionQuestions: What specific constraint would extraction remove?
Can module isolation solve the problem first?
What new failure and consistency problems would appear?
How would migration and rollback work?

learningJourney.title: Align software with the business
learningJourney.eyebrow: Domain modeling / One word, different meanings
learningJourney.purpose: Learn to model business responsibilities and define where each model applies.
learningJourney.explanation: A bounded context defines where a model and its language apply. Discover it by exploring real workflows with domain experts, rather than dividing entities into individual services.

ideas.title: Model the invariants
ideas.description: Entities have identity across changes. Value objects are defined by their values. Aggregates group state and behavior that must satisfy transactional rules.

ideas.title: Choose consistency boundaries
ideas.description: Keep an aggregate no larger than its invariants require. Changes across aggregates may need workflows or eventual consistency. One aggregate per transaction is a design guideline, not a universal database law.

example.title: A customer is not one universal object
example.scenario: Billing needs payment responsibility, shipping needs a recipient and address, and support needs interaction history.
example.reasoning: Each context can own its model and exchange only the facts it needs. An anti-corruption layer can translate foreign concepts instead of leaking them into the local model.
example.lesson: The same identifier or word does not imply shared model ownership.

reflectionQuestions: What does this business term mean in this context?
Who owns the rule and its authoritative state?
Which rules need immediate consistency?
Which external concepts need translation?

learningJourney.title: Separate rules from infrastructure
learningJourney.purpose: Structure code so business behavior does not depend directly on replaceable technology.
learningJourney.explanation: Clean, hexagonal, and onion architectures share a useful goal: core business policy should not depend directly on replaceable infrastructure. Define ports around application needs and implement adapters for HTTP, databases, queues, and vendors.

architectureFlow.name: Use case and domain
architectureFlow.description: Contains application workflows and business policy.

architectureFlow.name: Vendor adapter
architectureFlow.description: Translates the application contract to a provider SDK.

example.title: Replace a payment provider
example.scenario: Checkout currently uses one external payment provider but may need to support another.
example.reasoning: The charge-customer use case calls an application-level payment port. A provider adapter translates that request to the vendor SDK and maps its response into application terms.
example.lesson: Business decisions should not depend directly on one vendor's SDK.

caveats: Runtime calls may go outward even though source-code dependencies point toward application-defined contracts.
Do not add an interface around every class.
A fake adapter helps test business behavior but does not prove that the real provider integration works.
reflectionQuestions: Which code expresses business policy?
Which code only translates protocols or storage formats?
Can the use case run without the real database or vendor SDK?
Which dependency should be isolated behind an application-owned contract?

learningJourney.title: Choose how work crosses boundaries
learningJourney.purpose: Understand when to use synchronous calls, messages, and events, and how distributed data changes consistency.
learningJourney.explanation: Synchronous calls suit interactions that need an immediate answer. Asynchronous messages allow work to proceed independently but introduce delay, duplicate delivery, ordering, and operational state. Neither approach removes coupling.

communicationChoices.useWhen: The caller needs an immediate result.
A named capability should perform work later.
Consumers need to react to an already-committed fact.

example.title: Order placement starts a workflow
example.scenario: An order must be created while inventory reservation, payment, and notification may involve separate systems.
example.reasoning: Commit the order and an outbox record in one local transaction. A relay publishes the event. Consumers handle duplicates safely. A saga reserves inventory and charges payment, with business compensation if a later step fails.
example.lesson: A saga is not a global atomic transaction. Compensation is business work and can fail too.

ideas.title: Keep data ownership explicit
ideas.description: Services should not bypass one another's contracts by writing shared tables. Private ownership can exist within a shared database server; separate hardware is not always necessary.

ideas.title: Separate read needs when useful
ideas.description: A history projection can consume events into a query-friendly model. That is CQRS. Event sourcing, in which the event history is authoritative, is a separate optional decision.

caveats: A transactional outbox closes the local database and event-record gap.
Event publication may happen more than once, so reliable relaying, monitoring, and idempotent consumers are still needed.
A distributed workflow must account for failed compensation and uncertain outcomes.
reflectionQuestions: What identifies the logical operation?
Where is deduplication persisted?
How does the user interface describe a pending order?
What happens if compensation repeatedly fails?

learningJourney.title: Design for load and partial failure
learningJourney.eyebrow: Scale and resilience / Bound the blast radius
learningJourney.purpose: Identify constrained resources, control admitted work, and preserve important functionality when dependencies fail.
learningJourney.explanation: Scaling is not simply adding instances. Find the constrained resource, control admitted work, and define which capabilities survive when a dependency is slow or unavailable.

ideas.title: Reduce avoidable work
items: Cache reusable reads with explicit freshness bounds.
Batch operations when doing so reduces overhead.
Move email and reporting off critical request paths.
Account for replica lag when adding read capacity.

ideas.title: Bound resource consumption
items: Propagate deadlines and use finite timeouts.
Retry only safe operations within a bounded budget.
Use backoff and jitter instead of immediate retry loops.
Apply concurrency limits, bulkheads, and load shedding.

example.title: No recommendations is better than no checkout
example.scenario: A recommendations dependency becomes slow or unavailable.
example.reasoning: Give recommendations a short deadline and independent concurrency budget. Open a circuit breaker when failure thresholds are reached. Omit recommendations or use an explicitly permitted cached result while checkout continues.
example.lesson: Fault isolation requires resource limits and a fallback policy, not just separate services.

caveats: A queue buffers bursts but cannot handle unlimited demand. Bound backlog and monitor message age.
Serverless functions need downstream concurrency limits.
Durable state should not depend on ephemeral function memory.
reflectionQuestions: What is the critical user capability?
Which workloads share its connection or worker pools?
Which data may be stale, and for how long?
What is the retry budget for a request?

learningJourney.title: Operate, measure, and evolve
learningJourney.purpose: Connect architecture decisions with deployment, observability, reliability targets, and ongoing learning.
learningJourney.explanation: Architecture earns its value in production. Translate quality goals into measurable targets, test contracts and boundaries, deploy compatibly, and use incidents as evidence for the next decision.

ideas.title: Observe user outcomes
ideas.description: Define service-level objectives for success rate and latency. Track traffic, errors, saturation, and tail latency. Correlate structured logs and traces across synchronous and asynchronous boundaries.

ideas.title: Protect evolution
ideas.description: Use contract tests, schema compatibility checks, and automated dependency rules in CI. Roll out changes gradually and define rollback.

example.title: A new dependency slows checkout
example.scenario: A checkout request becomes slower after a downstream dependency is introduced.
example.reasoning: Tracing locates the added wait. Metrics show elevated p99 latency and resource saturation. Compare the result with the checkout SLO, reduce the dependency's resource budget or remove it from the critical path, then validate the change.
example.lesson: Diagrams suggest a design; telemetry shows how it behaves.

caveats: Audit authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, sensitive-data handling, and retention across boundaries.
These quality attributes are architectural requirements, not a final checklist after scaling.
Error-budget policies should guide priorities rather than become an automatic universal feature ban.
reflectionQuestions: Which user-visible outcome has a measurable target?
What boundary rule can CI enforce?
How would you safely test a dependency outage?
What incident evidence would cause you to revisit an architecture decision?

endToEndExample.title: Put the order platform together
endToEndExample.scenario: The system must accept orders, reserve inventory, charge customers, send notifications, and serve order history.

architectureFlow.name: Ordering
architectureFlow.responsibility: Owns the order and records an outbox event in the same transaction.

architectureFlow.name: Projection and notification consumers
architectureFlow.responsibility: Build order history and send notifications asynchronously.

reasoning: Ordering owns order transitions; inventory owns reservations; payment owns charges.
These logical boundaries do not all need to be separate deployments.
Record the accepted order and outbox event in one local transaction.
Coordinate downstream work with persisted workflow state, retries, and compensations.
Build order history asynchronously and keep notifications off the checkout path.
Monitor workflow age, duplicate handling, failed compensation, and user-visible completion.
lessons: A domain boundary should own both behavior and the data needed to enforce it.
Not every module needs to become a service.
Events and sagas relocate complexity into delivery, ordering, duplication, and compensation.
Resilience is part of architecture, not merely an infrastructure feature.
The simplest architecture that satisfies current requirements is usually the best starting point.

failureScenario.title: Payment times out after it may have succeeded
failureScenario.reasoning: Do not issue a new charge with a new operation identity. Reuse the original idempotency key and reconcile with the payment provider. Keep the workflow in an explicit uncertain state until authoritative status is known.
failureScenario.recovery: Define retries, reconciliation, and manual escalation for persistent ambiguity.

decisionFramework.question: What capability and invariant are we protecting?
decisionFramework.reason: Start from business behavior rather than a technology preference.

decisionFramework.question: Who owns the data and contract?
decisionFramework.reason: Explicit ownership avoids hidden writers, cross-team schema dependencies, and ambiguous authority.

decisionFramework.question: What consistency and communication are actually required?
decisionFramework.reason: Require immediate answers only when the business needs them.

decisionFramework.question: What happens under failure and overload?
decisionFramework.reason: Specify deadlines, bounded resources, retries, degradation, and recovery.

decisionFramework.question: How can the decision be verified and reversed?
decisionFramework.reason: Use measurable targets, migration seams, compatibility checks, and production feedback.

knowledgeCheck.question: A checkout application has six engineers and changing product requirements. The team proposes ten services to be ready for scale. What is the strongest first response?

options.text: Use ten services now; service count is a good measure of scalability.
options.feedback: Service count does not establish scalability. First identify workload constraints, business boundaries, and the operational cost of independent deployments.

options.text: Establish module boundaries, measure constraints, and extract services when concrete needs justify it.
options.feedback: Correct. Start with clear modular boundaries and measurable constraints. Extract services when ownership, scaling, deployment, or fault-isolation benefits justify the distributed-system cost.

options.text: Keep one application forever; distribution is always unnecessary.
options.feedback: Too absolute. A modular monolith is a useful starting point, not a permanent rule. Independent scaling, ownership, or reliability needs may later justify service extraction.

exercises.title: Model a commerce application
exercises.prompt: Identify responsibilities, data owners, invariants, and transactions before proposing any services.
reviewQuestions: Can each boundary be justified by change, ownership, or consistency?
Did you separate a logical module boundary from a deployment boundary?
Which shared models might create coordination costs?

exercises.title: Extract reporting safely
exercises.prompt: Explain the extraction trigger, read-model strategy, output validation, gradual rollout, rollback, and new operational risks.
reviewQuestions: Which system remains authoritative during the transition?
How will you compare old and new outputs?
Could rollback silently discard new state?

exercises.title: Recover a partially completed order
exercises.prompt: Inventory is reserved, payment status is uncertain, and notifications are unavailable. Describe workflow state, retries, reconciliation, compensation, and user messaging.
reviewQuestions: How do you avoid creating a duplicate charge?
How do you represent uncertainty to the user?
Can notifications recover independently from order processing?

domainContent.finalSummary: Good architecture is a set of justified decisions. Start from business responsibilities, keep ownership explicit, distribute only when it provides concrete value, design failure behavior deliberately, and use production evidence to evolve the system.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Good architecture makes changing your mind less expensive. Start with clear boundaries, explicit ownership, and controlled communication.

tipsAndTricks: Domain principle: Good architecture makes changing your mind less expensive. Start with clear boundaries, explicit ownership, and controlled communication.
End-to-end lesson: A domain boundary should own both behavior and the data needed to enforce it.

**Failure check — Payment times out after it may have succeeded:** Do not issue a new charge with a new operation identity. Reuse the original idempotency key and reconcile with the payment provider. Keep the workflow in an explicit uncertain state until authoritative status is known. **Recovery:** Define retries, reconciliation, and manual escalation for persistent ambiguity.
